title: Propagating fronts of convection rolls in Rayleigh-Bénard convection
abstract: We investigate the propagation of counter-rotating convection rolls in Rayleigh-Bénard convection initiated locally in a quiescent fluid layer under supercritical conditions. The velocity of the front separating quiescent fluid from the forming convection rolls, and the wavenumber of the convection rolls remaining behind the front, are explored. We numerically investigate fronts of forming convection rolls over five orders of magnitude of the reduced Rayleigh number, $ε$, in 2D and 3D domains, for a broad range of boundary conditions, and for different front initiation approaches. In all cases, the front velocity increases as $ε^{1/2}$ with increasing $ε$ for $ε\lesssim 1$ in agreement with predictions using the amplitude equation. The amplitude equation description of the front velocity remains accurate for $ε\lesssim 10$ except when the Prandtl number is large which yields a velocity that is faster than predicted for a fluid layer far from threshold. The wavenumber of the convection rolls increases linearly with $ε$ in agreement with the wavenumber that maximizes the growth rate of perturbations in the linear regime. Farther from onset, the wavenumber growth transitions to a reduced scaling of $ε^{1/4}$ in agreement with predictions using the Swift-Hohenberg equation in the large $ε$ limit. The scalings describing the wavenumber variation with $ε$ are independent of the domain geometry, boundary conditions, and front initiation method. However, the front-selected wavenumber at criticality does not equal the critical wavenumber of the bulk instability, in general, and depends significantly upon these details. We compare our results with experimental measurements where possible.
summary: This paper numerically analyzes how convection roll fronts propagate in Rayleigh-Bénard convection, determining scaling laws for front velocity and wavenumber. Key findings show that the front velocity scales as $\epsilon^{1/2}$ near onset, while the wavenumber scaling transitions from linear to $\epsilon^{1/4}$ further from threshold. The work is significant for understanding pattern selection in non-equilibrium physical systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the dynamics and scaling laws governing the propagation of fronts of convection rolls in Rayleigh-Bénard convection under supercritical conditions.
main_result: The front velocity scales as $\epsilon^{1/2}$ for small supercriticality ($\epsilon \lesssim 1$), while the wavenumber exhibits different scaling behaviors ($\epsilon$ vs. $\epsilon^{1/4}$) depending on the distance from onset.
method: The research employs detailed numerical simulations in 2D and 3D using a spectral element approach, comparing results against amplitude equation predictions and experimental data.
model_or_system: The physical system is Rayleigh-Bénard convection in a shallow fluid layer, governed by the Boussinesq equations. The focus is on the propagating front separating quiescent fluid from the forming convective rolls.
key_observables: Front velocity ($v_f$) and the wavenumber ($q$) of the convection rolls.
important_parameters: Reduced Rayleigh number ($\epsilon$), Prandtl number ($	ext{Pr}$), and domain geometry/boundary conditions.
main_assumptions: The front dynamics are studied before the bulk instability fully develops, and comparisons are made assuming ideal boundary conditions (e.g., perfect thermal conductivity).
figures_summary: The notes describe setups for 2D, 3D box, and cylindrical domains illustrating the geometry of the convection front propagation.
paper_structure: The paper systematically explores the front dynamics by varying the dimensionality (2D vs 3D), the geometry (box vs cylinder), and the method of front initiation, while comparing scaling laws to theory and experiments.
why_interesting: While focused on classical fluid dynamics, the study of pattern selection, front propagation, and universal scaling laws ($\epsilon^{1/2}$, $\epsilon^{1/4}$) shares mathematical similarities with pattern formation problems studied in non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and reaction-diffusion systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: 2D domain used to study the propagation of fronts of straight parallel rolls. A ﬂuid layer of length L and depth d with a hot bottom wall at Th (red) and cold top wall at Tc (blue) where Th > Tc. The front is initiated using a hot wall located as x = 0 (red) and propagates from left to right. The aspect ratios Γ = L/d used in the simulations are Γ = 30 and 60. Gravity opposes the z-direction.

Figure 2: A box domain with ﬁns attached to the sidewalls. (a) A ﬂuid layer of depth d with a rectangular cross section of lengths Lx and Ly in the x and y directions, respectively to yield Γx = Lx/d and Γy = Ly/d. The bottom wall is hot (red) and the top wall is cold (blue). Thin ﬁns are attached to the sidewalls (shown in gray). The front is initiated at the wall located at x=0 (red) and propagates in the positive x-direction. (b) A y–z cross-section highlighting the ﬁn geometry. The ﬁns are no-slip surfaces of ﬁnite thickness in the y and z-directions and are perfect thermal conductors. We also use a box domain without ﬁns (not shown) which is this domain with the gray ﬁns removed....

Figure 3: Cylindrical domain used to study the propagation of concentric convection rolls. A ﬂuid layer of depth d, radius r0, and aspect ratio Γ=r0/d with a hot bottom wall (red) at Th and cold top wall (blue) at Tc. All material boundaries are no-slip surfaces. The front is initiated at the origin by introducing a thermal perturbation at t=0. The front on concentric convection rolls propagates radially outward from the origin toward the sidewalls. Gravity opposes the z-direction and in our study Γ=40.

Figure 4: The temperature variation of a ﬂuid layer containing a front in a 2D domain forming a chain of counter-rotating convection rolls. Simulation parameters: Sim. 1, Γ=60, Ra=1745, Pr=1. (a) Color contours of T(x, z) at four times, the front propagates from left to right. The region 0≤x≤20 is shown for clarity. Red is hot rising ﬂuid and blue is cool falling ﬂuid. Time increases from top to bottom. (b) Temperature proﬁles T(x, z =1/2) as a function of time t. Time increases from bottom to top. The bottom curve is at t = 0, the interval between the remaining proﬁles is 5.68 time units.

Figure 5: Color contours of temperature (left column) and normalized stream function (right col- umn) for fronts in a 2D domain. Each row is for a diﬀerent value of Ra and shows contours at the time when xf = 24. The spatial region 13 ≤x ≤26 is shown for clarity. (a),(e) Ra = 2000; (b),(f) Ra=3300; (c),(g) Ra=5000; (d),(h) Ra=104. Simulation parameters: Sim. 1, Γ=30, Pr=1.
